analysis.one_liner: Bans corporations and unions from funding election ads and caps donations to Super PACs.
analysis.headline: Introduced March 21, 2013 with 17 Democratic cosponsors, the bill was referred to the House Administration Committee the same day and saw no further action before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would return to the rules that existed before the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision: corporations, national banks, and labor unions could no longer pay for political ads or make independent expenditures in federal elections. It would also apply existing contribution limits to Super PACs, which today can accept unlimited donations. In doing so, the bill reasserts Congress's claimed authority to limit election spending by corporate treasuries and union funds, drawing on earlier bans like the Tillman Act of 1907 and the pre-2010 reading of the Taft-Hartley Act.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters, who would face a political landscape in which corporate treasuries, banks, and union funds could no longer bankroll election ads, and in which Super PACs would be subject to the same contribution limits as other political committees. Candidates would be pushed to rely more on individual donors and less on a small pool of very large givers, which the bill's own findings note were 159 donors giving nearly 59 percent of Super PAC money in 2012.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits national banks, corporations, and labor organizations from paying for electioneering communications — the broadcast ads run just before an election that mention a federal candidate — closing a channel through which unlimited corporate and union money currently reaches voters [S2][S3].
Bans independent expenditures by corporations and labor organizations, directly reversing the effect of the Citizens United decision for federal elections [S2][S3].
Applies standard contribution limits to money given to Super PACs, or to any political committee or account that accepts noncompliant funds, ending their ability to take unlimited checks [S2][S3].

The bill's findings cite polling that large majorities want limits on campaign money, including one poll finding 89 percent of Americans believe there is too much money in politics, and note that 31 percent of 2012 outside spending could not be traced to its original source [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations, national banks, and labor unions lose their post-Citizens United ability to spend treasury money on federal elections, and the wealthy donors and Super PAC operators who accepted unlimited contributions would be subject to ordinary campaign finance limits.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations, banks, unions, and Super PAC donors

drawbacks.text: The Supreme Court held in Citizens United v. FEC (2010) that the First Amendment bars exactly this kind of ban on corporate and union independent expenditures, so major provisions would likely face immediate constitutional challenge; the bill itself carries a severability clause anticipating that parts could be struck down [S3].

The ban applies symmetrically to labor unions as well as corporations, so unions would lose the ability to fund political advertising and independent spending with member dues money, not just corporate treasuries [S2][S3].

The bill carves out exceptions for 501(c)(4) nonprofits and other political organizations funded exclusively by individual citizens, which in practice could allow large individual donors to keep influencing elections through those channels rather than eliminating the problem [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing corporate treasury and union money from federal elections and capping Super PAC donations — addresses the problem the bill's own findings document: outside spending dominated by a few hundred megadonors and untraceable dark money. The chief weakness is that the same Supreme Court precedent that opened the door to this spending would likely strike down the ban in court, making the bill partly symbolic unless the Court reversed course or the Constitution were amended. The union side of the ban also cuts against a significant progressive constituency, and the individual-funded 501(c)(4) carve-out leaves a loophole for wealthy individuals. Even so, the practical effect on election spending would be large if it were ever enforced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. John Dingell on March 21, 2013 and referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration [S1][S5].
Seventeen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; the record shows no Republican cosponsors [S4].
The full action history contains only two entries — introduction and referral — with no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action at any point during the 113th Congress [S5].

Republicans held the House majority in the 113th Congress, and the House Administration Committee is chaired by the majority party, so the committee that controlled the bill's fate did not act on it [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations, national banks, labor unions, and the Super PAC megadonors keep their ability to spend unlimited money on federal elections; no voter-facing limits were enacted.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; the record shows no Republican support, and the Republican-controlled committee and majority never scheduled action on the bill.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to spend treasury money on federal election ads and independent expenditures, a right they gained through Citizens United. Their interest in that spending runs directly against the bill's stated goal of limiting the influence of concentrated money over elections.

industries.industry: Super PACs and their large donors
industries.note: Standard contribution limits would replace unlimited donations, ending the channel through which 159 donors supplied nearly 59 percent of Super PAC money in 2012. The bill is aimed squarely at this concentration of giving.

Unions would be banned from spending dues money on election ads and independent expenditures exactly as corporations would, restoring the pre-2010 ban on both sides. Unions' interest in spending on elections runs against the bill's limits, though the bill treats unions and corporations symmetrically.

The bill allows them to keep spending if they use only segregated funds from individual citizens, but bars them from targeted broadcast ads that reference candidates other than the President or Vice President and from using any corporate or business-derived funds. Some dark-money channels would close; others would remain open.
